notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for **Mark 2**, drawn from the sources reached.

---

## Mark 2:1–12 — The Healing of the Paralytic

### v. 1 — "A few days later Jesus went back to Capernaum. And when the people heard that He was home…"

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus returned to Capernaum after a preaching tour through Galilee (Mk 1:35–45). Mark alone names the town; Matthew calls it "His own city" (Mt 9:1). "Home" is widely taken to be Peter's house (see Mk 1:29), which had become Jesus' base of operations in Galilee. Despite Jesus' attempt to stay in "unpopulated areas" after the leper's healing (Mk 1:45), His presence could not be hidden.
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm
— Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-2-commentary

**Reformed (R.C. Sproul / Ligonier):** Sproul notes that Jesus returned from His preaching tour and immediately crowds gathered, showing His fame.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-healing-paralytic

### v. 2 — "…they gathered in such large numbers that there was no more room, not even outside the door, as Jesus spoke the word to them."

**Traditional Reading:** Mark's vivid detail ("not even outside the door") is one of his characteristic touches. The phrase "spoke the word" (literally, "He was speaking the word") emphasizes Jesus' primary mission: preaching, not just healing. Stedman (cited in Enduring Word) suggests Jesus was avoiding the streets because they had become "a healing campaign" that hindered His preaching ministry.
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

### v. 3 — "Then a paralytic was brought to Him, carried by four men."

**Traditional Reading:** Only Mark records the number of bearers (four). The detail highlights the effort and cooperation of the man's friends.
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm
— Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-2-commentary

### v. 4 — "Since they were unable to get to Jesus through the crowd, they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat."

**Traditional Reading:** Palestinian homes typically had flat roofs accessible by an outside staircase, constructed of beams covered with thatch, dirt, or tile. Mark's language is strong: they "dug through" or "broke up" the roof (Gk. *exoryxantes*). Morgan comments that "they broke up the roof of the house, tearing up the fabric." The determination demonstrated visible faith — having lowered the man, they counted on him walking out, since pulling him back up would be far harder.
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm

### v. 5 — "When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus "saw" their faith — faith visible through bold, determined action. Significantly, Jesus addressed the man's deepest need first: forgiveness, not physical healing. As Wiersbe says (cited in Enduring Word), "Forgiveness is the greatest miracle that Jesus ever performs. It meets the greatest need; it costs the greatest price; and it brings the greatest blessing and the most lasting results." Jesus did not mean the man was especially sinful or that his paralysis was caused by specific sin; He addressed the common root of all suffering — the fallen, sinful human condition.
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

**Reformed (R.C. Sproul / Ligonier):** Sproul emphasizes that "there is nothing in the text that suggests the man was looking for forgiveness. He was looking for healing." Jesus went deeper than the paralysis to the man's deepest need: relief from guilt. The greatest thing that happened to the paralytic that day "was not the healing of his body; it was the forgiveness of his soul."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-healing-paralytic
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/forgiveness-and-healing

### vv. 6–7 — "But some of the scribes were sitting there and thinking in their hearts, 'Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?'"

**Traditional Reading:** The scribes' logic was theologically correct — only God can forgive sins (cf. Ps 130:3–4; Isa 43:25). Their error was refusing to recognize *who* Jesus is: God the Son. Cole (cited in Enduring Word) notes: "Again and again during the life of Christ the same dilemma was to reappear. If he were not divine, then he was indeed a blasphemer; there could be no third way out." The better manuscripts give: "Why does this man thus speak? He blasphemeth."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm

**Reformed (R.C. Sproul / Ligonier):** Sproul explains that every scribe knew the principle in Judaism that no man, not even the Messiah, would have authority to forgive sins — that was God's prerogative alone. So if Jesus were merely a man, the charge of blasphemy would stick. But Christ, though fully human, is not *merely* human; He is God incarnate.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-healing-paralytic
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/christs-divine-authority

### v. 8 — "At once Jesus knew in His spirit that they were thinking this way within themselves. 'Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?' He asked."

**Traditional Reading:** Mark's mention that Jesus perceived this "in His spirit" is unique to his account. Ellicott notes this as significant "in its bearing on the reality and completeness of our Lord's human nature." Trapp (cited in Enduring Word) finds basis for either divine knowledge or the spiritual gift of discernment.
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

### vv. 9–11 — "'Which is easier: to say to a paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven," or to say, "Get up, pick up your mat, and walk"? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…' He said to the paralytic, 'I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.'"

**Traditional Reading:** The logic is: it is "easier" to say "your sins are forgiven" because no one can verify it visibly. But if Jesus can do the visible, verifiable miracle (healing), He proves He also has authority for the invisible one (forgiveness). Jesus uses the title "Son of Man" — a reference to Daniel 7:13–14, a Messianic title free from political/nationalistic overtones. Robertson notes it was "Christ's favourite designation of himself, a claim to be the Messiah in terms that could not easily be attacked."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/
— JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/mark/2.htm

**Reformed (R.C. Sproul / Ligonier):** Sproul explains that the easier option seems to be saying "your sins are forgiven" because no visible test can falsify it. But Jesus chose to put Himself to the test by healing the man, thereby vindicating His claim to forgive sins. Calvin adds: "As it is not easier to quicken by a word a body which is nearly dead than to forgive sins, there is no reason to wonder that he forgives sins, when he has accomplished the other."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-healing-paralytic
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/christs-divine-authority

### v. 12 — "And immediately the man got up, picked up his mat, and walked out in front of them all. As a result, they were all astounded and glorified God, saying, 'We have never seen anything like this!'"

**Traditional Reading:** The healing was instantaneous and complete. The man carried the very bed that had carried him — Bengel remarks, "Sweet saying! The bed had borne the man: now the man bore the bed." The crowd's reaction ("We have never seen anything like this") is rendered by Luke as "We have seen strange things today." The scribes' logic was hoist with their own petard: on their own stated beliefs, a man could not be cured unless forgiven. He was cured; therefore he was forgiven; therefore Jesus' claim was true.
— JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/mark/2.htm
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

## Mark 2:13–17 — The Calling of Levi and Eating with Sinners

### vv. 13–14 — "Once again Jesus went out beside the sea… He saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. 'Follow Me,' He told him, and Levi got up and followed Him."

**Traditional Reading:** Levi (also called Matthew; cf. Mt 9:9) was a tax collector — a profession despised by Jews as both traitors (working for Rome) and extortioners (they could keep whatever they over-collected). Tax collectors were disqualified as judges or witnesses, excommunicated from synagogues, and their disgrace extended to their families (Lane). Jesus' call to Levi was remarkable love. Enduring Word notes that Levi's was "a sacrifice harder than the other disciples made because Levi could never return to his old job."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm

### vv. 15–17 — "While Jesus was dining at Levi's house, many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Him… 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Most regard this as a farewell banquet Levi threw for his associates. Table fellowship in that culture signified friendship and acceptance — hence the scandal. The Pharisees ("separated ones") objected to Jesus keeping company with those they deemed unholy. Jesus' answer — "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners" — is both simple and profound: as the physician of the soul, it makes perfect sense for Him to be with the sin-sick. Notably, Mark and Luke (writing for Gentiles) omit Matthew's reference to Hosea 6:6 ("I desire mercy, not sacrifice").
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm

## Mark 2:18–22 — The Question about Fasting

### v. 18 — "Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were often fasting. So people came to Jesus and asked, 'Why don't Your disciples fast like John's disciples and those of the Pharisees?'"

**Traditional Reading:** Pharisees typically fasted twice weekly (Lk 18:12). John the Baptist's disciples fasted as part of his repentance-focused ministry. The question implies criticism: why did Jesus' disciples not display the same devotional rigor?
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

### vv. 19–20 — "Jesus replied, 'How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?… But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus used the analogy of a wedding — during the weeklong Jewish wedding celebration, rabbis declared that joy trumped religious ritual. By calling Himself the bridegroom, Jesus made a profound claim: in the OT, God pictured Himself as the husband of Israel (Isa 62:4f; Jer 2:2; Ezek 16:8; Hos 2:19f). Jesus was claiming to be the divine Bridegroom. Fasting would resume when He was "taken away."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

**Baptist/Reformed (John Piper / Desiring God):** Piper emphasizes that Jesus' coming as the Bridegroom is "too good to mingle with fasting." Jesus was making a "tremendous claim" — "God, the one who betrothed Israel to himself in covenant love, has come." The "days will come" refers to the present church age: Jesus has returned to the Father, and now is the time for fasting. However, Piper argues that Christian fasting is *new* fasting — not the old Jewish fasting. It "rests on all this finished work of the Bridegroom. The yearning that we feel for revival or awakening… is not merely longing and aching. The first fruits of what we long for have already come."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/when-the-bridegroom-is-taken-away-they-will-fast-with-new-wineskins

### vv. 21–22 — "No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment… And no one pours new wine into old wineskins…"

**Traditional Reading:** The two illustrations make the same point: Jesus came to introduce something genuinely new that cannot be contained within the old forms of Judaism. Unshrunk cloth shrinks and tears away from the old garment. New wine ferments and expands; old wineskins have already stretched and become brittle — they burst under the pressure. Jesus didn't come to "patch up" the old system but to fulfill it. Enduring Word: "Jesus traded fasting for feasting; sackcloth and ashes for a robe of righteousness… mourning for joy; and law for grace."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

**Baptist/Reformed (John Piper / Desiring God):** Piper argues that the old wineskin in context is fasting — specifically, the old Jewish understanding of fasting. The new wine is the kingdom of God that has come in Christ. "The old wineskins of Judaism can't contain the new wine." But Jesus doesn't abolish fasting; He transforms it. "The new wine demands new fasting" — fasting that is based on the mystery that the Bridegroom *has come*, not merely that He *will come*. Christian fasting rests on the finished work of Christ and is shaped by the presence of the kingdom already inaugurated.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/when-the-bridegroom-is-taken-away-they-will-fast-with-new-wineskins
— https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-do-christians-fast

## Mark 2:23–28 — Lord of the Sabbath

### vv. 23–24 — "One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain… 'Look, why are they doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?'"

**Traditional Reading:** Gleaning from a neighbor's field was permitted by Deuteronomy 23:25. The issue was not theft but Sabbath violation. The Pharisees' elaborate oral tradition treated the disciples' actions as four violations: reaping, threshing, winnowing, and preparing food. Enduring Word details the absurdity of rabbinic Sabbath rules: one could not tie a knot but a woman could tie her girdle to a bucket; one could not carry something in the right hand but could with the back of the hand, elbow, or ear.
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

### vv. 25–26 — "'Have you never read what David did…? During the high priesthood of Abiathar, he entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread…'"

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus cites 1 Samuel 21:1–6, where David and his men ate the showbread (reserved for priests) when hungry. The principle: human need outweighs ceremonial regulation. The reference to "Abiathar" creates a historical difficulty since 1 Samuel 21:1 names Ahimelech as the high priest at that time; Abiathar was his son who later served as high priest. Ellicott offers two explanations: (1) Abiathar was the more famous priest and his name was used; or (2) Abiathar may have acted as coadjutor to his father and was the chief agent in allowing David to take the bread.
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/

### vv. 27–28 — "'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Two principles are established. First, the Sabbath was created by God to serve and bless humanity — not to enslave it. Any application of Sabbath law that harms people contradicts God's purpose (Morgan). Second, Jesus claims ultimate authority over the Sabbath as "Son of Man" — a title drawn from Daniel 7:13–14 that asserts His Messianic lordship. If He is Lord of the Sabbath, He has the right to interpret and apply it correctly.
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-2/
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/2.htm

**Denominational Note — Sabbath/Lord's Day differences:** Protestant traditions differ on how this passage applies to the Christian Lord's Day. Reformed confessions (Westminster, Heidelberg) tend to see a binding moral principle of one-day-in-seven rest carried forward, though the day changed to Sunday in honor of the resurrection. Lutheran and many evangelical traditions emphasize that the Sabbath command was a ceremonial law fulfilled in Christ and that vv. 27–28 free believers from legalistic Sabbath-keeping. Baptist teaching varies, but generally stresses the principle of rest and worship without the OT ceremonial restrictions.
